name: HD 110067 b
significanceText: The innermost of six sub-Neptunes that all still move in near-perfect step with each other, like they've barely changed since the day they formed.

name: HD 110067 c
significanceText: Orbits its star twice for every three trips b makes — a tidy little rhythm that's held steady for billions of years.

name: HD 110067 d
significanceText: Astronomers worked out this planet had to exist just from the system's orbital math, then found it right where they expected.

name: HD 110067 e
significanceText: Predicted on paper before it was ever seen — the resonance pattern basically told astronomers where to look.

name: HD 110067 f
significanceText: Another planet that theory found first — its orbit fell exactly where the resonant chain said it should.

name: HD 110067 g
significanceText: The outermost of the six, taking its time — one leisurely orbit for every six the innermost planet squeezes in.

name: K2-138 b
significanceText: Found by ordinary people scrolling through telescope data on their laptops — the first exoplanet system ever discovered that way.

name: K2-138 c
significanceText: One link in the longest unbroken chain of orbital near-resonances known at the time — spotted by volunteers, not professionals.

name: K2-138 d
significanceText: Part of a five-planet find that citizen scientists pieced together within weeks of the project going live.

name: K2-138 e
significanceText: Circles its star in a little over eight days, one more link in a system that regular people helped uncover from home.

name: K2-138 f
significanceText: The fifth planet in the crowdsourced find, closing out a strikingly neat resonant chain at just under 13 days.

name: K2-138 g
significanceText: Turned up a year later in leftover data, sitting outside the tidy chain — a hint there may be even more planets hiding here.

name: TOI-178 b
significanceText: The odd one out — every other planet here dances in resonance, but this innermost world sits just outside the rhythm.

name: TOI-178 c
significanceText: A dense, rocky world sitting right next door to a much puffier planet — a mismatch that still puzzles formation theories.

name: TOI-178 d
significanceText: Light and gassy where its neighbor c is dense and rocky — right next door to each other, but built completely differently.
